clue.text: Expression of surprise after Catholic’s brought in a drink

indicators.note: something brought in is carried inside, so one piece goes into another

explanation.surface: Someone gasps as a Catholic friend arrives carrying a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is a decoy: the Catholic letter goes inside the exclamation rather than following it. Coo is a mild British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot beverage made from powdered cacao beans, usually with milk.

clue.text: Palace attendant having no time for messenger

indicators.note: having none of something means that letter is taken away, and time is the usual abbreviation T

blocks.note: someone who attends a royal court

explanation.surface: A royal servant is reassigned from palace duty to carrying messages.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the T (time) from COURTIER to leave COURIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A courier carries letters, parcels or dispatches from one person to another, which is exactly the job of a messenger.

clue.text: Dance is more attractive when carrying a hat

indicators.note: whatever is carried is held inside, so one piece goes within another

explanation.surface: A fashion claim that a dance looks better when the dancer wears a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The comparative adjective splits after its first three letters to take in the hat, and the break lands neatly on the first word of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut a caper is an idiom meaning to leap or frolic about playfully, a lively kind of dancing.

clue.text: Idiot singer missing introduction

indicators.note: lacking an introduction means the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: a singer with the lowest male voice

explanation.surface: A foolish performer forgets to begin the song properly.
explanation.walkthrough: BASS loses its B to give ASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ass is an informal insult for a foolish, stupid person, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Founding Father, fellow causing annoyance mostly

indicators.note: most but not all means the final letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A complaint that a revered founder of a nation was mostly an irritant.
explanation.walkthrough: F plus RANKLING without its last G.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Franklin was one of the statesmen who signed the Declaration of Independence and shaped the United States.

clue.text: The fortune possibly revealed in day associated with lovers?

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may be reordered

explanation.surface: A fortune teller predicts luck on Valentine's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition works by example: the day is not named, only its date.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Valentine's Day, when romantic couples exchange cards, falls on February the 14th.

clue.text: Grass found in local farms

indicators.note: what is found in something sits inside the printed letters, waiting to be spotted

blocks.note: runs across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A particular grass grows on nearby farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across locAL FArms.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfa is another name for esparto, a tough North African grass used to make paper and rope.

clue.text: Percussion section to become quieter? It’s generally kept out of everything

definitions.text: It’s generally kept out of everything

blocks.note: orchestral slang for the percussion department
a voice sinks when it drops in volume

explanation.surface: A conductor's instruction for the drummers to play softer, then a general remark about something left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Orchestral players call the percussion section 'the kitchen', for all its pots and pans; this is the obscure step.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'everything but the kitchen sink' describes taking nearly all things, with only that basin left behind.

clue.text: One unclear about love language?

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece wraps another

explanation.surface: Someone confused about romance, groping for words.
explanation.walkthrough: I then DIM wrapped around O; the surface idiot pulls toward the wrong word.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is the particular vocabulary or manner of speech of a people or region, so a language in that sense.

clue.text: Account incorporating information on company’s latest operation

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body, so one piece holds another
the latest of a sequence is its final item, so keep the last letter
in a down entry, placing one thing on another sets it below it in the grid

blocks.note: British slang for information, as in 'the gen'

explanation.surface: A report that includes details on a firm's most recent business activity.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British slang for facts or information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Agency means action or the means by which something is done, the working of a force, much like an operation.

clue.text: Excellent, having moved on from other forms of tobacco?

definitions.text: having moved on from other forms of tobacco?
definitions.note: a cryptic phrase, read as advanced as far as snuff

blocks.note: straight sense: meeting the required standard

blocks.clueFragment: having moved on from other forms of tobacco?
blocks.note: whimsical sense: having worked through pipes and cigars up to the powdered kind

explanation.surface: Praise for a smoker who has progressed beyond cigarettes to something else.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the phrase literally: someone who has gone through other tobaccos and reached snuff, the powdered tobacco sniffed up the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to snuff is an idiom for good enough or of an acceptable, high standard.

clue.text: Difficult to dismiss source of regret in a draw

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, so take its first letter
dismissing sends something away, so a letter is removed

explanation.surface: Sportspeople find it hard to shrug off disappointment after a drawn match.
explanation.walkthrough: TRYING loses its R.
explanation.definitionFit: Two sides tying finish level on points, the same result as a drawn contest with no winner.

clue.text: Foster popular suggestion about cricketer

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: a batsman is often called a bat

explanation.surface: A popular idea about a cricket player named Foster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foster' looks like a surname in the surface but is the verb; a batsman is routinely called a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: To incubate an idea or egg is to nurture and develop it, the same as to foster its growth.

clue.text: One enjoying the sun, getting nasty about lake, threatened landowner

indicators.note: getting something means adding it on, so one piece follows another
about means going around, so one piece encloses another

explanation.surface: A sunbather turns unpleasant near a lake and menaces a landowner.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition needs the novel: Sir Henry Baskerville is the heir menaced by a spectral dog in Conan Doyle's The Hound of the Baskervilles.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry, the Dartmoor squire in the Sherlock Holmes story, is stalked by a supposedly cursed hound.

clue.text: Magician pretended to take a name

indicators.note: taking something on means adding it, so pieces join end to end

explanation.surface: A conjuror adopts a false stage name.
explanation.walkthrough: SHAM plus A plus N.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaman is a priest or healer believed to wield spiritual powers, a kind of sorcerer or wizard.

clue.text: Heroic men at sea bringing in dead marine creature

indicators.note: bringing something in takes it inside, so an extra letter joins the group
at sea means confused and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Brave sailors haul a dead sea animal aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Add D to HEROIC MEN and rearrange all ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Echinoderms are the phylum of spiny-skinned ocean animals such as starfish and sea urchins.

clue.text: TV presenter from part of London blocking mature response

indicators.note: East End Cockney speech drops its aitches, so an H goes
something blocking a passage sits in the middle of it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the person who fronts a show

explanation.surface: A television presenter from a London district stands in the way of a grown-up reply.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney, the working-class dialect of London's East End, famously drops the letter H, so the presenter loses an initial H as a Cockney would say it.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick, clever reply, originally a fencing counter-thrust, so a sharp retort.

clue.text: Clamour to include lively tune in collection of one hundred

indicators.note: lively suggests energetic movement, so the letters jump into a new order
including something means holding it within, so one piece goes inside another

explanation.surface: Fans demand that an upbeat song be added to a compilation of a hundred tracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lively tune' reads as a song, but only the second word is fodder; the first tells you to mix it.
explanation.definitionFit: A century is any set of a hundred, such as a hundred runs in cricket or a hundred years.

clue.text: Ruins veal after cooking without exception

indicators.note: cooking changes raw ingredients into something new, so the letters are remixed

explanation.surface: A chef ruins the veal every single time.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an adjective; 'without exception' fits phrases like 'a rule applying without exception'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something universal applies to all cases everywhere, leaving none out.

clue.text: Working to turn around hospital drama

indicators.note: turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Staff work to rescue a hospital TV drama.
explanation.walkthrough: ON flipped to NO, then H. 'Hospital drama' reads as one phrase, but the two words do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Noh is the classical Japanese theatre form using masks, music and dance.

clue.text: What tailor provides: good skill around chaps

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one piece wraps another

explanation.surface: A tailor's craft is to fit clothes well around male customers.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon separates the definition from the wordplay; everything before it is a descriptive definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailor makes and supplies items of clothing, and a garment is any such piece of clothing.

clue.text: Acquired guy from the country, not entirely romantic

indicators.note: not quite whole means the final letter is cut

explanation.surface: Someone takes up with a rustic fellow who is only half a romantic.
explanation.walkthrough: GOT plus HICK without its K. 'Romantic' is the literary sense, not the amorous one.
explanation.definitionFit: Gothic fiction, with its gloomy castles and heightened emotion, belongs to the Romantic movement in literature.

clue.text: I’m collecting free iodine, uranium and another element

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so other pieces go inside

blocks.note: to free of something is to rid

explanation.surface: A chemist boasts of gathering spare iodine and uranium, plus a third element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' nods to the two elements already named in the surface; the answer is a third.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridium is a dense, hard metal in the platinum group of the periodic table, symbol Ir.

clue.text: Drink supplier’s exploit having a lot of people running short

indicators.note: being short of supply means the final letter is missing

blocks.note: to take advantage of, as in 'milk the situation'

explanation.surface: A drinks vendor boasts of a feat, with many customers queuing as stock runs low.
explanation.walkthrough: MILK plus MANY without its Y. In Britain milkmen still deliver bottles to doorsteps.
explanation.definitionFit: A milkman delivers bottles of milk to homes, so he provides a beverage.

clue.text: Do well dividing four into three? Not entirely

indicators.note: not quite complete means the last letter is dropped
something that divides splits a thing apart by sitting inside it

explanation.surface: A maths puzzle about how well four goes into three.
explanation.walkthrough: The arithmetic surface is a decoy: four is a Roman numeral and three is the word itself, clipped at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrive is to flourish and prosper, the same as succeeding or doing well.

clue.text: Feature of many a poem? "Hard to fill lines" - the writer

indicators.note: filling something means going inside it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
railway, the lines trains run on

explanation.surface: A poet complains that it is hard to fill out lines with verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' looks like lines of verse but is the railway; 'the writer' is the setter, giving the first-person pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyme, matching sounds at the ends of lines, is a common device in verse though not every poem uses it.

clue.text: Popular music genre’s comfortable for American artist

blocks.note: the genre, with the 's read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A particular pop style suits an American painter.
explanation.walkthrough: ROCK plus WELL; 'comfortable' is in the sense of being well enough off.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Rockwell was an illustrator and painter famed for his Saturday Evening Post covers of small-town US life.

clue.text: Panic mostly produces evidence of trauma

indicators.note: most but not all means the final letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A fright leaves lasting psychological harm.
explanation.walkthrough: SCARE without its last E.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the mark left on skin after a wound heals, so a visible sign of past injury.

clue.text: A delightful experience? Wrong to pen diary without content

indicators.note: emptying out the inside leaves only the outer letters
penning something in encloses it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: ill as in wrong or harmful, 'ill-advised'
first and last letters of diary

explanation.surface: A lovely time spent, but it's wrong to write an empty diary entry about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hints the definition is loose rather than exact: an idyll is often a scene or poem, not only an experience.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is an extremely happy, peaceful or picturesque episode or scene, often romanticised.

clue.text: Tight dress flaunted in chosen mag?

indicators.note: something flaunted is shown off in a new display, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A figure-hugging dress is shown off in a selected fashion magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: An unfamiliar word, so the fodder is the route in: rearrange CHOSEN MAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheongsam, or qipao, is a close-fitting Chinese dress with a high collar and slit skirt.

clue.text: Leg up offered in hurry

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: slang for a leg, as in 'wobbly on my pins'

explanation.surface: Someone gets a boost when in a rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg up' reads as help; split it, and the second word works on the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To nip is British informal for going somewhere quickly, as in 'nip to the shops'.

clue.text: Spirits after cold beer befuddled the brain

indicators.note: a befuddled mind is muddled, so the letters are mixed up
one thing coming after another places it later in the answer

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a spirit distilled from sugar cane

explanation.surface: Drinking spirits on top of chilled beer leaves a person's head fuzzy.
explanation.walkthrough: C, then BEER rearranged, then RUM, though the clue lists the spirits first.
explanation.definitionFit: The cerebrum is the largest, front part of the brain, handling thought and movement; the whole stands for a major part.

clue.text: Supporter of lines partly gutted - no line put back

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, so only the outer letters stay
putting something back returns it the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: first and last letters of partly

explanation.surface: A cable mast's crew leaves a job half done, never replacing a line.
explanation.walkthrough: PY, then NO plus L reversed. 'Partly' is the word being gutted, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A pylon is a tall steel tower that carries overhead electricity cables across country.
